newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao summoned to face vote-buying charges.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao summoned to face vote-buying charges.

text.p: An Indian judge on Friday ordered former Indian Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao to appear in court later this month to face vote-buying charges, as the beleaguered political leader's legal troubles deepened.
Judge Ajit Bharihoke ordered Rao to appear on November 13 in the three-year-old case, one of three that have ensnared the Congress party leader and stirred political uncertainty.
Bharihoke had the choice of summoning Rao or issuing an arrest warrant, court officials said. He chose merely to summon Rao to appear with co-defendants in the case of alleged bribery.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) indicted Rao and six others on Wednesday for allegedly conspiring to pay $100,000 to legislators from a regional party to vote against a 1993 no-confidence motion that Rao's Congress Party narrowly won.

Rao has also been charged with criminal forgery in a case stemming from 1989. The CBI claims Rao conspired to defame rival politician V.P. Singh by using false documents to make it appear Singh and his son had violated foreign exchange rules.
Rao appeared before chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar twice this week in the forgery case, the first former or serving prime minister to appear in court to face criminal charges.
Last month Rao was arrested in the case, then immediately released on temporary bail.
Kumar is set to rule on Tuesday on Rao's request for an extension of the temporary bail, which has protected him against arrest in the case but which expires on Wednesday.

Rao has been named but not charged in a third case of criminal conspiracy to cheat. He quit as Congress party chief in September after Bharihoke upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court to face criminal cheating charges.
Bharihoke has set a trial hearing in the case for next Wednesday.
As his legal troubles have multiplied, pressure has mounted on Rao to relinquish his last political post as head of the Congress party's parliamentary delegation.

Rao was replaced as party president by Sitaram Kesri, an apostle of Mahatma Gandhi who has taken a more forceful stance than Rao in dealing with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front ruling coalition.
Deve Gowda's minority government depends on Congress's backing to thwart potential challenges by Hindu nationalists in parliament.

A struggle for power in Uttar Pradesh after inconclusive general elections has stoked tension between Congress and the United Front, which are backing rival local politicians for the chief ministership of the state, India's most populous.
Kesri has repeatedly said Deve Gowda cannot take Congress's support for granted.
"They (the United Front) think they are powerful. But the fact is that they are ruling on our strength," the Times of India quoted Kesri as saying at a public rally on Thursday.
"This 13-party government thinks it can lecture us. They will have to listen to us," Kesri was quoted as saying.
